title: Thermal energy transfers and the greenhouse effect
summary: Temperature and internal energy, specific heat and latent heat, conduction, convection and radiation, black-body radiation laws, and Earth’s energy balance and the greenhouse effect.

keyterms.definition: Total random kinetic energy plus intermolecular potential energy of the particles in a substance.
A measure of the average random kinetic energy of particles; T(K) = θ(°C) + 273.
Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K: Q = mcΔT.
Energy needed to change the phase of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature: Q = mL.
Thermal energy transfer through a material by particle collisions (and free electrons in metals); rate = kAΔT/Δx.
Thermal energy transfer by bulk movement of a fluid caused by density differences.
An ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits the maximum possible radiation for its temperature.
Power radiated by a black body: L = σAT⁴.
Peak emission wavelength is inversely proportional to temperature: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.
Ratio of power emitted by a surface to that of a black body at the same temperature (0 to 1).
Fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects; Earth’s mean albedo is about 0.3.
Warming of a planet’s surface because atmospheric gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, some back towards the surface.
Intensity of the Sun’s radiation at Earth’s mean distance, about 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻², above the atmosphere.

lessons.title: Heating, phase change and energy transfer

questions.prompt: How much energy is needed to heat 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 70 °C? (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)

questions.statement: While ice melts at 0 °C, its temperature stays constant even though energy is supplied.
questions.explanation: The energy increases intermolecular potential energy (breaking bonds), not the mean kinetic energy, so temperature is constant.

questions.text: The energy needed to melt 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C (L_f = 3.3 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹) is ___ kJ.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is directly related to the average kinetic energy of the particles in a gas?
questions.explanation: Temperature in kelvin is proportional to the mean random kinetic energy of the particles.

questions.text: A temperature of 27 °C is equal to ___ K.

questions.prompt: Match each process to its mechanism.

pairs.right: Bulk fluid flow driven by density change
Electromagnetic waves, works in a vacuum
Fastest particles escape a liquid surface

questions.explanation: Each mechanism transfers thermal energy in a different way.

questions.prompt: The rate of conduction through a wall is given by kAΔT/Δx. Doubling the wall thickness, other factors unchanged, makes the rate
questions.explanation: Rate ∝ 1/Δx, so a wall twice as thick conducts at half the rate.
Convection needs bulk movement of the material, so it happens only in fluids (liquids and gases).

questions.prompt: Equal masses of two liquids receive the same energy. Liquid X warms by 10 K, liquid Y by 5 K. Compared with Y, X has
questions.explanation: c = Q/(mΔT); a larger ΔT for the same Q and m means a smaller c, here half.

questions.prompt: Order the stages as a block of ice at −10 °C is heated steadily to steam at 100 °C.
questions.explanation: Temperature rises in single-phase stages and stays constant during each phase change.

lessons.title: Radiation, black bodies and Earth’s energy balance

questions.prompt: The Sun’s surface temperature is about 5800 K. Using Wien’s law, its peak wavelength is about
questions.explanation: λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / 5800 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm, in the visible region.

questions.statement: If the absolute temperature of a black body doubles, the power it radiates increases by a factor of 16.
questions.explanation: L = σAT⁴, so L ∝ T⁴ and 2⁴ = 16.

questions.text: Earth’s surface (about 288 K) radiates most strongly in the ___ region of the spectrum.
questions.explanation: λ_max = 2.9 × 10⁻³/288 ≈ 10 µm, which is infrared.

questions.prompt: A planet absorbs sunlight and has an albedo of 0.30. What fraction of the incident radiation does it absorb?
questions.explanation: Albedo is the reflected fraction, so 1 − 0.30 = 0.70 is absorbed.

questions.prompt: Why is the average intensity of sunlight absorbed over Earth’s whole surface about S/4 × (1 − albedo)?
options: Earth intercepts sunlight over a disc of area πR² but radiates from a sphere of area 4πR²
The Sun is four times further away at night
Only a quarter of the surface is land
questions.explanation: Intercepted power = SπR²(1 − α); spreading it over 4πR² gives S(1 − α)/4.

questions.text: A body with emissivity e radiates power P = eσA___.
questions.explanation: Real surfaces emit a fraction e of black-body power: P = eσAT⁴.

questions.statement: Greenhouse gases absorb most of the incoming visible sunlight before it reaches the surface.
questions.explanation: They are largely transparent to visible light but absorb outgoing infrared, re-emitting some back to the surface.

questions.prompt: Why can molecules such as CO₂ and H₂O absorb infrared radiation?
options: Infrared frequencies match the natural frequencies of their molecular vibrations
questions.explanation: Resonance: infrared photons excite bending and stretching vibrations in these molecules.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Emission compared with a black body
Intensity of sunlight at Earth’s distance

questions.explanation: These quantities appear in simple energy-balance models of Earth.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of the greenhouse effect.
items: Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun reaches the surface
The surface warms and emits infrared
Greenhouse gases absorb some of the infrared
The gases re-emit infrared in all directions, partly back to the surface
questions.explanation: The returned infrared means the surface is warmer than it would be with no atmosphere.
